hints: Focus on what must happen first before any precipitate can form, the C-X bond has to break in water to release a halide ion.
Recall the trend in carbon-halogen bond strength, C-F is very strong and hard to break while C-I is very weak and breaks easily.
Compare the halogens present in each molecule and ask which molecule contains the halogen that is released most easily as $X^-$ to react with $Ag^+$.
walkthrough:
**Understand the test**

Warming a halogenoalkane with water hydrolyses it slowly. Then the halide ion formed gives a precipitate with silver ions.

$$R-X + H_2O \rightarrow R-OH + X^- + H^+$$
$$Ag^+(aq) + X^-(aq) \rightarrow AgX(s)$$

**Identify the rate-determining factor**

The quickest precipitate comes from the compound that releases $X^-$ fastest. That depends on how easily the $C-X$ bond breaks.

Bond strength decreases down Group 17: $C-F$ > $C-Cl$ > $C-Br$ > $C-I$. So $C-I$ hydrolyses fastest and $C-F$ hardly hydrolyses at all.

**Compare the four compounds**

Compound A has only $C-Cl$ bonds. Compound B has $C-Cl$ and $C-F$. Compound D has $C-Br$, $C-Cl$ and $C-F$. Only one compound contains a $C-I$ bond, the weakest of all.

That $C-I$ bond breaks most readily on warming, releasing $I^-$ quickly to form yellow $AgI$ precipitate. So that compound is the quickest.

options.A: Contains three $C-Cl$ bonds only. $Cl^-$ is released by hydrolysis, but $C-Cl$ is much stronger than $C-Br$ and $C-I$, so precipitation is slower.
options.B: Contains one $C-Cl$ and two $C-F$ bonds. $C-F$ is extremely strong and does not hydrolyse under these conditions, so only the $C-Cl$ can react, which is slower than $C-Br$ or $C-I$.
options.C: Contains two $C-F$ bonds and one $C-I$ bond. The $C-I$ bond is the weakest carbon-halogen bond, so it hydrolyses fastest on warming to release $I^-$, which rapidly gives $AgI$ precipitate with $AgNO_3$.
options.D: Contains $C-Br$, $C-Cl$ and $C-F$. $C-Br$ hydrolyses faster than $C-Cl$, so this is faster than A and B, but $C-Br$ is still stronger than $C-I$, so it is slower than the iodo compound.
